4 min read 4 hours ago -- Press enter or click to view image in full size Gameweek #1 FPLI’ve been publishing my weekly Fantasy Premier League picks on a little site — Best XI, captain, transfers, differentials, a few reasons why. Nothing fancy. But building it, I noticed something I keep coming back to. Every instinct I had said: add a database. Add an API to serve the picks. Maybe a small CMS so updating is nicer, maybe an admin panel. That’s just what you reach for when you’re publishing something on a schedule, right? It’s the default shape a “content site” takes in your head before you’ve thought about it for more than five minutes. Except none of that was actually needed. What I publish every week is really just one file’s worth of facts — this week’s team, this week’s captain, this week’s transfers, a couple of differential picks, which fixtures look easy or brutal. It doesn’t change per visitor. It’s just this week’s facts, read by whoever shows up. So that’s what it is now: one JSON file per Gameweek, gw01.json through gw38.json, sitting next to a plain HTML page that reads it and paints itself. How a page actually gets built There’s no framework rendering anything. A player card is literally a JS function that concatenates strings and drops the result into innerHTML: function playerCardHtml(player) { const clubHex = RH.clubColor(player.club); return '
' + '
' + RH.formatValue(player.name) + '
' + '
' + RH.formatValue(player.reason) + '
' + '
'; }No virtual DOM, no diffing, no re-render cycle to think about — the page is built once per load and that’s the whole lifecycle. It sounds primitive written out like that, but for a page that’s read, not interacted with, there’s nothing a framework would actually be buying me. The one place I put real thought in was legibility: club colors tint each player’s jersey icon (no crests, no sponsor logos — just a color, which sidesteps a whole licensing question while still being recognizable), and the text on that badge picks black or white depending on the color’s actual brightness, computed with the standard relative-luminance formula rather than hardcoded per club. Small thing, but it’s the kind of detail that’s easy to skip on a “just render some JSON” project and then regret when Fulham’s white jersey swallows white text. The part that surprised me: testing a “static site” at all Everything genuinely computational — grouping players by position, sorting the bench by substitution order, formatting a date, building the FAQPage JSON-LD block — lives in one file, render-helpers.js, written so it exports itself two ways: as window.RenderHelpers in the browser, and via module.exports in Node. Same file, unmodified, runs in both places. That one trick is what let me write actual unit tests — with Node’s built-in test runner, node --test, zero dependencies — for logic that would otherwise only be verifiable by opening the page and squinting. No Jest, no bundler config, no jsdom setup. Just plain functions, tested as plain functions. The validator doing the job a schema library usually does Next to the JSON files sits a 200-ish line hand-written validator — no Zod, no Ajv, no JSON Schema library, just a script that walks each data/gwNN.json and checks that required keys exist, positions are one of GK/DEF/MID/FWD, isCaptain appears exactly once inside startingXI, and so on. It's blunt, but it means a typo in a hand-edited JSON file fails loud in a npm run validate-data run before it ever reaches a browser, instead of quietly rendering a blank captain card in production. The same shape-checking function gets reused for an optional unlimitedSquad field too — a second, no-budget-cap recommendation some weeks need and most don't — rather than writing a parallel validator for it. Even the SEO story stays static Each Gameweek’s HTML page is pre-generated once, for all 38 weeks, up front — permanent URLs that never move, which matters for a fantasy-football audience that might come back to “what did the site say for GW12” months later. On top of that, the render layer builds Article and FAQPage JSON-LD blocks client-side from the same JSON that renders the page, so structured data for search stays in sync with content automatically instead of being a separate thing to remember to update. Why any of this matters to me None of these are clever tricks on their own. What ties them together is that every one of them was a small “do I actually need infrastructure for this, or just a slightly better plain function” decision, made in the moment it came up, rather than reached for by default. A schema library instead of 200 lines of if-statements would’ve been more “correct” in some abstract sense. It also would’ve been a dependency, a version to bump, and a slightly bigger mental model for a project that’s supposed to take five minutes a week to update. The question that mattered every time was the same one: does this actually need to be dynamic, or does it just need to be correct? Most of what ends up as a database, an API, or a framework is really just that second thing, dressed up.
